clue.text: Some dish, says theatre's vox populi

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a stalk vegetable stewed as a pudding
second meaning: the word stage crowds mutter to sound like a hubbub of voices

explanation.surface: A dish being judged by the theatre's ordinary audience.
explanation.walkthrough: Extras in a crowd scene traditionally repeat 'rhubarb, rhubarb' to make a murmur of background talk.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant is cooked as a pudding, and its name is also the stock murmur of stage crowds.

clue.text: Apostasy, a job for a dog

definitions.meaning: first meaning: deserting one's side, as a rat leaves a sinking ship
second meaning: hunting vermin, as terriers do

explanation.surface: Abandoning one's faith described as dirty work fit only for a cur.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat is to desert or betray one's party, while terriers are bred for catching vermin.

clue.text: Freed to dance in the nude, perhaps

indicators.note: in tells us one piece is placed inside the other
perhaps hints that the word is only one possible arrangement of its letters

parts.note: taken as written
the twist, a 1960s dance

explanation.surface: Someone liberated enough to dance with no clothes on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the nude' reads as one phrase, but 'in' places the dance inside a rearranged 'nude'.
explanation.definitionFit: Untwisted means unwound or disentangled, so something untwisted has been released from its coils.

clue.text: Poplar's third man, note

parts.note: Abel, son of Adam, was the third human after his parents and brother Cain
a musical note

explanation.surface: A man who ranks third in Poplar, an East London district, plus a written memo.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads 'Poplar is', the apostrophe standing for the verb. Poplar is also a district of East London.
explanation.definitionFit: The abele is the white poplar, a tree with silvery leaves, so it is one type of poplar.

clue.text: Two drinking places, one an awfully rough one

parts.note: two pub bars
the Roman numeral for one, then the article as written

explanation.surface: A pub crawl of two bars, with one being a very rough joint.
explanation.definitionFit: A barbarian is an uncivilised, coarse and brutal person, so a very crude fellow.

clue.text: Clumsy fellows talk about ill-gotten gains

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: to gas is to chatter idly
plunder or stolen goods

explanation.surface: Awkward men chattering about money they came by dishonestly.
explanation.definitionFit: A galoot is slang for an awkward, oafish man, so the plural describes clumsy blundering chaps.

clue.text: A slip-up doesn't finish the foreman

indicators.note: something that doesn't finish stops short, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: gaffer is British slang for a boss or foreman

explanation.surface: A blunder means the works supervisor never completes the job.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaffe is an embarrassing blunder or social mistake, a tactless error.

clue.text: Bird sitting on eggs in the delphiniums

parts.note: a songbird
to egg on is to spur on, so eggs is the verb spurs

explanation.surface: A bird brooding its clutch in a flower bed.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the first piece sits on top of the second. 'Eggs' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Larkspur is the common name for annual delphinium plants, tall blue-flowered garden perennials.

clue.text: West — remarkable chap all round. He's got something

indicators.note: all round means encircling, so the chap wraps around the direction

parts.note: a oner is British slang for an exceptional person
the compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: Praise for a fellow from the West, an all-round marvel with a certain something.
explanation.definitionFit: An owner possesses property, so literally he is a man who has something of his own.

clue.text: Jack's up here to soak the French

parts.note: to steep is to soak in liquid
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A man called Jack climbs up somewhere to drench some French people.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack is not a person but half of steeplejack, the worker who climbs church towers.
explanation.definitionFit: A steeplejack works high on church spires, so the spire is where such a worker is found aloft.

clue.text: Championship of the right

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the status of champion, as in a boxing crown
second meaning: a legal claim to ownership, as in a deed to land

explanation.surface: A sporting crown being claimed as belonging to the rightful holder.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a sporting crown and a legal claim of ownership to property.

clue.text: Respect for a character

definitions.meaning: first meaning: regard, as in 'with respect to'
second meaning: a written testimonial about a person's character for an employer

explanation.surface: Someone earning esteem for their good nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In respect of' and 'with reference to' are interchangeable, and a character was the old term for a job testimonial.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both relation or regard and a testimonial letter vouching for someone applying for work.

clue.text: One point to consider in tour from place to place

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
a prong or spike, as of a fork or antler
to rate is to regard or judge

explanation.surface: A debating point to think about when planning a journey round several places.
explanation.definitionFit: To itinerate is to travel on a circuit, as preachers or judges once did when moving between towns.

clue.text: Runs in bar for a sharpener

indicators.note: in places the runs inside the word for bar

parts.note: to bar is to stop or block
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Someone dashing into a pub for an aperitif to sharpen the appetite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' and 'sharpener' paint a drink in a pub, but the bar is a verb and the sharpener a razor tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A strop is the leather strap barbers use to hone the edge of a cut-throat razor.

clue.text: Set for example in reverse gear

indicators.note: going in reverse means the pieces are read from right to left

parts.note: to set something down is to put it
the abbreviation of exempli gratia

explanation.surface: A driver told to put the car into reverse gear, by way of example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reverse gear' looks like a single motoring phrase; the reversal signal ends at 'reverse' and the outfit sense of gear is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A get-up is an outfit or costume, and clothes are informally called gear.

clue.text: Recantations by poet's friendly collaborator

parts.note: a pal is a friend
read as 'in odes', where a poet's work is found

explanation.surface: Retractions signed by a poet and their amiable co-writer.
explanation.walkthrough: The friend appears in the poet's verses: the poet's possession is read as being inside his odes.
explanation.definitionFit: A palinode is a poem retracting an earlier one, hence any formal withdrawal of a statement.

clue.text: Wire-pulling gets us a chimney in the pub by the church

indicators.note: a chimney in the pub is literally placed inside it

parts.note: an inn is a pub
a flue is the duct inside a chimney
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone working their contacts to get the pub by the church to sort out its chimney.
explanation.definitionFit: Wire-pulling is using private pull behind the scenes, which is exactly what influence means as a noun.

clue.text: Competitors — a passenger gets the bird

parts.note: the field is all the runners in a race
a taxi driver calls a passenger a fare

explanation.surface: The runners in a race, and a traveller who gets jeered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets the bird' is slang for being booed, but here the bird is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The fieldfare is a large thrush that winters in Britain, so it is a species of bird.

clue.text: Prison specified by friends so called

parts.note: nick is British slang for prison or police station
identified by name

explanation.surface: Which jail was identified by an inmate's mates.
explanation.definitionFit: A person nicknamed something is known by an informal label that intimates use instead of the real name.

clue.text: What made North once idle?

indicators.note: asking what something was made from invites rebuilding the following letters into a new word

parts.note: N is the compass abbreviation for north
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about why Lord North, the prime minister who lost America, was once so lazy.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: laziness is what makes anyone idle.
explanation.definitionFit: Indolence is laziness, the quality that leaves a person idle, which is what the question asks for.

clue.text: Put revenue on one side for the successor

parts.note: earnings
R for right, one side

explanation.surface: Setting money aside to provide for an heir.
explanation.definitionFit: An incomer is one who comes in to take the place of another, such as a new tenant replacing the last.

clue.text: Only ringing about the plinth

indicators.note: ringing means forming a ring around, so one piece encircles the other

parts.note: sole means single or only
C is circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A bell ringing only around the base of a statue.
explanation.definitionFit: A socle is the plain block forming the base under a column, statue or wall, which is a plinth.

clue.text: Made safe of course, finally

parts.note: in the end
'Sure!' is an exclamation meaning of course

explanation.surface: Something at last secured, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no word signalling the insertion: the second phrase simply sits within the last.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensure is to secure or guarantee, making something certain and safe from risk.

clue.text: Al's tail-less bird

indicators.note: without a tail, the final letter of the name is cut off

parts.note: Al Capone, the Chicago gangster

explanation.surface: A man named Al owns a bird that has lost its tail feathers.
explanation.definitionFit: A capon is a castrated cockerel raised for the table, so it is a domestic fowl.

clue.text: One point in young Fido's attractive picture

indicators.note: in puts the first pieces inside the young dog

parts.note: Fido is a stock dog's name, and a young dog is a pup
the Roman numeral for one
a compass point, north

explanation.surface: A detail in a puppy's charming photograph.
explanation.definitionFit: A pin-up is a picture of an attractive person, made to be pinned up on a wall.

clue.text: First principles — little cash in little pigs

indicators.note: the cash goes in the pigs, placed inside them

parts.note: a runt is the smallest pig in a litter
a dime is a small American coin

explanation.surface: Basic lessons in saving: put small coins in your piggy bank.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudiments are the elementary basics of a subject, the fundamentals one learns at the very start.

clue.text: Rob the old magistrate, say?

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the word and hear a different spelling

parts.note: a reeve was a medieval local official or magistrate

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to plunder the elderly judge.
explanation.definitionFit: To reave is an archaic verb meaning to plunder or take by force, the root of bereave.

clue.text: Chop logic perhaps, but do not so use words

definitions.meaning: first meaning: cut meat or vegetables very finely
second meaning: from the idiom 'not to ... words', speaking bluntly

explanation.surface: Advice to argue pedantically if you must, yet speak frankly.
explanation.walkthrough: To chop logic is to argue pedantically; the clue only borrows the verb, and someone who does not 'mince words' is blunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Mincing is cutting food into tiny pieces, and mincing words means softening what one says.

clue.text: Not long without a drink" — a solo performance

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a short while
no as in 'no money', lacking
a small measure of whisky
taken as written

explanation.surface: A one-person show whose title is a line about going briefly without a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' joins the dram at the end, not the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A monodrama is a play or dramatic piece written for a single performer.

clue.text: About a thousand railwaymen in Belgium

indicators.note: About means surrounding, so the union wraps around the first pieces

parts.note: the National Union of Railwaymen
taken as written
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Around a thousand railway workers posted to Belgium.
explanation.walkthrough: The NUR was the British rail workers' trade union.
explanation.definitionFit: Namur is a city and province of southern Belgium, so it is a place found there.

clue.text: Pointed reply in prose it might appear

indicators.note: the answer is how those letters might appear once rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sharp retort that could turn up in a piece of writing.
explanation.definitionFit: A riposte is a quick, sharp retort, originally the fencer's counter-thrust after a parry.

clue.text: Get half of them finished, corrected

indicators.note: half of a four-letter word keeps just two of its letters

parts.note: the second two of four letters
over, completed

explanation.surface: An instruction to get some of the jobs completed and put right.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend is to remove errors from a text, so emended means revised and set right.
